knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, 
                      fig.path = "figure-pbc/", fig.align = "center",

                      collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 104, digits = 4)

The goal of this vignette is to replicate the analysis of PBC data performed by [@Vavra-etal2024] with the use of `clustGLMM` package. 
This is the list of packages required for the analysis:

```{r library}
library(survival)
library(mixAK)
library(clustGLMM)
```


## PBC910

The sequential PBC data can be found in `pbcseq` from library `survival`. 
We restrict ourselves only to patients who survived the first 910 days (2.5 years) similarly as [@KomarekKomarkovaJSS14mixAK], who created `PBC910` data in library `mixAK`.
However, we need more columns than `PBC910` provides so we create our `data` from `pbcseq` by taking the same rows as `PBC910`. 

```{r pbc-data}
data(PBC910, package = "mixAK")
data(pbcseq, package = "survival")
data <- merge(PBC910, pbcseq, by = c("id", "day", "platelet", "spiders"))
dim(data)
(n <- length(unique(data$id)))      # number of subjects in the data
```

Next we prepare the outcomes for analysis:
```{r data-transformations}
data$ord_edema <- factor(data$edema, ordered = TRUE)
data$lalbumin <- log(data$albumin)
data$time <- data$day/365.24
```
```{r data-transforms-additional, echo = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# Appeared in the old R file, only if needed
data$ord_stage <- factor(data$stage, ordered = TRUE)
data$lalk.phos <- log(data$alk.phos)
data$lplatelet <- log(data$platelet)
data$lchol <- log(data$chol)
data$fage <- cut(data$age, breaks = c(0, 40, 50, 60, 80))
data$fage2 <- cut(data$age, breaks = c(0, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 80))
```

The analysis in the paper consisted of 

* numeric serum bilirubin and albumin (both on log-scales), 
* binary indicators of blood vessel malformations in the skin (`spiders`) and presence of hepatomegaly or enlarged liver (`hepato`),
* ordinal `edema` (0 = no edema, 0.5 = untreated or successfully treated, 1 = edema despite diuretic therapy).

We create `family` argument to declare the type of the considered outcomes for `clustGLMM` analysis:
```{r family}
family <- c(lbili = "num", platelet = "poi", spiders = "bin")
```

The formulas for analysis will be the same for all outcomes.
The fixed effects part will be an additive model with linear effect of `time` and `age` adjusted for different `sex`.
All these effects are assumed to be group-specific.
Finally, outcomes are joined via random intercepts.
```{r formula}
formula <- list()
for (y in names(family)) {
  formula[[y]] <- list()
  formula[[y]]$fixed <- ~ 1 # will become ~ 0
  formula[[y]]$group <- ~ time # + age + sex
  formula[[y]]$random <- ~ 1 + time
}

formula$spiders$fixed <- ~ time
formula$spiders$group <- ~ 1
formula$spiders$random <- ~ 1
```

Below we show the summary of the variables considered within this analysis:
```{r data-summary}
summary(data[, c("time", "age", "sex", names(family))])
```
We see that some of the binary outcome values are missing.
However, for `clustGLMM` there is no need for omitting the rows from the analysis as long as the missing values are among modelled outcomes. 

Now we examine how does the outcome evolve in time:
```{r plot-pbc-vs-time}
par(mfrow = c(1,3))
par(mar = c(4,4,1,0.5))
plot_num_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "lbili", x = "time", id = "id")
plot_num_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "platelet", x = "time", id = "id")
plot_cat_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "spiders", x = "time", main = "spiders")
```


## Sampling MCMC using `clustGLMM`

Some of the key inputs for `clustGLMM` are already prepared (`family`, `formula`), 
but there still some key settings to be discussed. 
Non-effects parameters of the model may also be set to be group-specific.
The default setting is provided by
```{r varying}
(varying <- default_varying())
```
Only precision of the errors of numeric outcomes and ordered intercepts are considered to be group-specific parameters by default.
We set the precision matrix (`InvSigma`) of the vector of random intercepts to be group-specific as well,
but keep its Wishart prior scale matrix `InvQ` common to all groups. 
Missing outcome values will be always predicted for the current cluster the individual is assigned to. 
```{r varying-InvSigma}
varying["prec_num"] <- TRUE
varying["InvSigma"] <- TRUE
```


Next, we can choose which parameters are returned. 
We make just one change compared to the default setting and that is to save the predicted missing values.
```{r save}
save <- default_save()
save["naY"] <- TRUE
```

For `tuning` we will use settings that and `param` will be kept without any changes. 
```{r tuning}
tuning <- default_tuning(experience = TRUE)
param <- default_param(sparse = TRUE)
# param[["prec_num_shp"]] <- 0.001
# param[["prec_num_rte"]] <- 1
# param$InvV <- 0.00000001
# param[["beta_num_fix_sd"]] <- 10
# param[["beta_num_sd"]] <- 10
# data$platelet <- round(data$platelet / 100)
```


Since we do not know the number of underlying clusters in advance, 
we set the maximal number of clusters `G` to 5.
We also apply standardization of covariates and outcomes to ensure that priors are truly non-informative. 
We run a couple of randomly initialized chains for initial 1000 iterations.

```{r clustGLMM-burnin}
set.seed(123456789)
mcmc_burnin <- clustGLMM(formula = formula, id = "id", family = family, data = data,
                         G = 10, nchains = 2, iter = 1000, 
                         varying = varying, save = save, tuning = tuning, param = param,
                         standardize = FALSE)
```

The default `plot` output informs us about the evolution of number of patients within each cluster separately for all chains:
```{r plot-mcmc-burnin}
plot(mcmc_burnin)
```

Apparently the number of non-empty groups is decreasing in time. 
Moreover, it seems to differ between chains: 
```{r plot-mcmc-burnin-Gplus}
plot(mcmc_burnin, "Gplus")
```

The current chains cannot be used for inference.
We continue to sample from initial values set to `mcmc_burnin$last`:

```{r clustGLMM-burnin2}
mcmc_burnin <- clustGLMM(formula = formula, id = "id", family = family, data = data,
                         G = 10, nchains = 2, iter = 1000, 
                         inits = mcmc_burnin$last,
                         varying = varying, save = save, tuning = tuning, param = param,
                         standardize = TRUE)
```

And we plot the same plots again to see that one chains prefers the two-cluster solution while the other still keeps 3 clusters while one of the clusters is rather sparse. 

```{r plot-mcmc-burnin2}
plot(mcmc_burnin)
```

Now we sample next $10\,000$ iterations.

```{r clustGLMM}
mcmc <- clustGLMM(formula = formula, id = "id", family = family, data = data,
                  G = 10, nchains = 2, iter = 10000, 
                  inits = mcmc_burnin$last,
                  varying = varying, save = save, tuning = tuning, param = param, 
                  standardize = TRUE)
```

```{r plot-mcmc}
plot(mcmc)
```

```{r plot-mcmc-clusters-kde}
ch <- 1
plot(mcmc, "beta_num", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "beta_bin", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "beta_ord", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "c_ord", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "sdSigma", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "corSigma", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
plot(mcmc, "w", "clusters_kerneldensity", chain = ch)
```

```{r post-processing}
mcmc_pp <- post_processing(mcmc)
```


```{r Uclustering}
data[,paste0("Uclustering", ch)] <- mcmc$clustering[as.character(data$id),ch]
```



```{r plot-pbc-vs-time-clustered, fig.height = 6}
par(mfrow = c(1,3))
par(mar = c(4,4,1,0.5))
plot_num_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "lbili", x = "time", group = "Uclustering1", id = "id")
plot_num_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "platelet", x = "time", group = "Uclustering1", id = "id")
plot_cat_vs_x_grouped(data, y = "spiders", x = "time", group = "Uclustering1", main = "spiders")
```

## Vignette tutorial 

Vignettes are long form documentation commonly included in packages. Because they are part of the distribution of the package, they need to be as compact as possible. The `html_vignette` output type provides a custom style sheet (and tweaks some options) to ensure that the resulting html is as small as possible. The `html_vignette` format:

- Never uses retina figures
- Has a smaller default figure size
- Uses a custom CSS stylesheet instead of the default Twitter Bootstrap style

### Vignette Info

Note the various macros within the `vignette` section of the metadata block above. These are required in order to instruct R how to build the vignette. Note that you should change the `title` field and the `\VignetteIndexEntry` to match the title of your vignette.

### Styles

The `html_vignette` template includes a basic CSS theme. To override this theme you can specify your own CSS in the document metadata as follows:

    output: 
      rmarkdown::html_vignette:
        css: mystyles.css

### Figures

The figure sizes have been customised so that you can easily put two images side-by-side. 

```{r, fig.show='hold'}
plot(1:10)
plot(10:1)
```

You can enable figure captions by `fig_caption: yes` in YAML:

    output:
      rmarkdown::html_vignette:
        fig_caption: yes

Then you can use the chunk option `fig.cap = "Your figure caption."` in **knitr**.

### More Examples

You can write math expressions, e.g. $Y = X\beta + \epsilon$, footnotes^[A footnote here.], and tables, e.g. using `knitr::kable()`.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(head(mtcars, 10))
```

> "He who gives up [code] safety for [code] speed deserves neither."
